title: Review: Oxidation states and naming; Born–Haber cycles and lattice enthalpy; Enthalpies of solution and hydration; Entropy
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EN06#t4 term and clue written for the game; EN06#t2 term and clue written for the game; EN07#t4 term and clue written for the game; EN06#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN06#N.4, EN07#N.13, EN08#N.4, RX02#N.4a, EN06#N.13, EN07#N.5, EN08#N.10b, RX02#N.10, RX02#N.8. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Born–Haber cycle
items.clue: Hess's law applied to an ionic solid, drawn as an energy-level diagram.

items.label: First ionisation energy
items.clue: ΔH when 1 mol of gaseous atoms each lose one electron: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻.

items.label: Exothermic
items.clue: Dissolving of this kind makes the water warmer: more energy is released than absorbed.

items.label: Enthalpy of atomisation
items.clue: ΔH when 1 mol of free gaseous particles such as Na(g) forms from an element in its standard state.

questions.stem: Which equation, with the sign of its enthalpy change, represents the enthalpy change of lattice formation of sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: One mole of solid forms from its gaseous ions. The ions attract, so energy is released: negative.

questions.stem: A student stirs potassium nitrate, KNO₃, into water in an insulated cup. The temperature falls from 21.0 °C to 14.5 °C. Which statement explains the fall?

options.text: Water molecules surrounding the ions absorb energy from the water, cooling it.
Separating the ions releases energy, but not enough to warm the water.
Separating the ions absorbs more energy than ion–water attractions release.
The dissolving salt releases energy to the water, which lowers its temperature.

questions.explanation: The energy to break up the solid outweighs the energy released by the new ion–water attractions. The difference is taken from the water, so it cools: dissolving KNO₃ is endothermic.

questions.stem: Which change has a negative entropy change, ΔS, for the system?
questions.explanation: Two moles of gas become one, so there are fewer ways to arrange the particles and their energy: ΔS is negative.

questions.stem: What are the oxidation numbers of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In NaH, Na is +1, so H is −1 (the hydride ion). In Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so O is −1 (the peroxide ion, O₂²⁻).

questions.stem: For which compound would you expect the largest percentage difference between the Born–Haber lattice enthalpy and the value from a perfect ionic (purely electrostatic) model?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ is small and doubly charged, so it polarises strongly. I⁻ is large, so its electron cloud is easily distorted. Most covalent character, biggest gap.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the enthalpy change of hydration of magnesium ions?
questions.explanation: One mole of gaseous Mg²⁺ ions is surrounded by water. Strongly exothermic.

questions.stem: Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, dissolves in water at room temperature, and the solution gets colder. Which statement best explains why this endothermic change still happens?

options.text: The water cools, so its molecules become more ordered, and this ordering drives the change.
Dissolving is really exothermic; the fall in temperature on the thermometer is misleading.
Breaking up the ammonium nitrate lattice releases energy, which pushes the ions into solution.
The ions spread from an ordered lattice through the water, so disorder (entropy) increases.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.
2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = +12, so each Cr is +6. The numeral is per atom.
